title: Weak Verbs: Names and Classes
description: Name a weak verb by the position of its weak letter.

blocks.caption: Summary
blocks.html: A weak verb has a weak letter among its three root letters: a guttural (א, ה, ח, ע, and for some purposes ר), a quiescent (א, ה, ו, י), or נ. Weak verbs are named by the position of the weak letter, using the letters of the model verb פָּעַל: פ for the first root letter, ע for the second, ל for the third.

blocks.caption: Naming by פ, ע, ל
blocks.html: נָפַל (fall) is a Pe-Nun verb, its first letter נ; יָשַׁב (sit) is Pe-Yod; קוּם (rise) is Ayin-Waw, or hollow; שָׁמַע (hear) is Lamed-Guttural; גָּלָה (uncover) is Lamed-He. א and ה are gutturals at the start of a root and quiescents at the end, so הָלַךְ (go) is Pe-Guttural but גָּלָה Lamed-He, and אָסַף (gather) is Pe-Guttural but מָצָא (find) Lamed-Aleph. A few verbs whose א falls silent in the imperfect, like אָמַר (יֹאמַר), are called Pe-Aleph. A verb whose second and third letters are the same, like סָבַב (go around), is Double-Ayin.

blocks.caption: More than one weak letter
blocks.html: A verb with two weak letters is named after both: יָדָה (throw, praise) is Pe-Yod and Lamed-He. Each weak letter follows its own rule.

blocks.caption: Not irregular
blocks.html: "Irregular" is a misnomer. The weak verbs follow the regular paradigm, changed in predictable ways by their weak letter. A Piel cannot double a guttural middle letter, so בֵּרַךְ (he blessed) lengthens the vowel before the ר instead of doubling it. Learn the rules for gutturals, quiescents, and נ, and the forms follow.

blocks.caption: Common confusion
blocks.html: Do not memorize weak verbs as exceptions. Name the root's weak letters first, then apply each one's rule: a missing letter (יִפֹּל from נפל) or a changed vowel (בֵּרַךְ) is the rule at work.
